raw_response:
**My thinking:**

I've been farming this same land in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and corn here, his father before him. The soil is good flat plain land — it suits nothing better than winter wheat and summer maize, one right after the other. That's the rotation. Everyone in the village does it. I do it.

I have 8 mu of land total. After the wheat comes off in June, I plant corn on the same ground. Two crops, same field, same year. This is how we survive.

For wheat, I'll buy improved seed from the village cooperative supply station — the Jimai variety they've been selling for years, not the old seed I'd save myself. My neighbor tried saving seed two years ago and his yield dropped. I won't do that. For corn, I buy hybrid seed from the agri-supply store in town. Everyone uses hybrid now. You get much better ears.

Fertilizer: I put down compound fertilizer as the base when I till, then come back with urea when the wheat is jointing. For corn I side-dress urea when it's knee-high. I don't measure carefully — I go by what the bags say and what I've learned to do.

Irrigation: I share access to the village pump well. Wheat needs water four times — before winter freeze, at jointing, at heading, and at grain fill. Corn I water once or twice if the summer rains are poor, which they often are here.

For corn I won't bother tilling again — I just direct-seed right into the wheat stubble with the small planter. Saves time and diesel.

I won't try anything new this year. Cotton prices are unpredictable. Vegetables need more work and a truck to sell them. At my age, with my back, wheat and corn is what I know and what I'll do.
